content.text: Unit 3 Overview

Unit 3 is the largest and most heavily weighted unit in AP CSP — 30–35% of the exam. It covers variables, lists, data abstraction, expressions, Boolean logic, conditionals, loops, algorithm design, searching, procedures, libraries, randomness, simulations, efficiency, and the limits of computation. Every topic is directly testable. This review hits the most important concepts and common exam traps for all 18 topics.
Topics 3.1 and 3.2 — Variables, Lists, and Data Abstraction

content.definition: An abstraction inside a program that can hold a value. The value stored will always be the most recent value assigned. Variables can hold numbers, Booleans, lists, and strings.

An operator that allows a program to change the value represented by a variable. It evaluates the expression on the right and assigns a copy of the result to the variable on the left. The value stored in a variable will always be the most recent value assigned.

content.term: What happens when a variable is assigned a new value?
content.definition: The value stored in a variable will always be the most recent value assigned. Example: if a = 1, then b = a, then a = 2, displaying b still shows 1 because b was assigned a copy of a's value at that time.

content.text: The most critical rule: when b ← a executes, b receives a COPY of a's current value. If a changes later, b is completely unaffected. Always evaluate the right side fully before assigning to the left side variable.

content.code:
a ← 5
b ← a        -- b gets a COPY of a's value (5)
a ← 10       -- a changes, b is unaffected
DISPLAY b    -- displays 5, NOT 10
DISPLAY a    -- displays 10

-- Multi-step trace:
x ← 3
y ← x + 2   -- y = 5
x ← y * 2   -- x = 10 (y still 5)
y ← x - y   -- RIGHT side first: 10-5=5, then y=5
DISPLAY x   -- 10
DISPLAY y   -- 5

content.definition: Numbers, Booleans, lists, and strings. Some values are better suited to representation using one type of datum rather than another.
An ordered sequence of elements. Each element is assigned a unique index starting at 1. Allows multiple related items to be treated as a single value. Also called an array in some languages.

A common method for referencing elements in a list or string using natural numbers. In AP CSP, indices start at 1. Accessing an index less than 1 or greater than the list length produces an error and terminates the program.

Giving a collection of data a name without referencing the specific details of its representation. Using lists allows multiple related items to be treated as a single value, making programs easier to develop and maintain.
An ordered sequence of characters. String concatenation joins two or more strings end-to-end to make a new string. A substring is part of an existing string.

content.term: How does assigning one list to another work?
content.definition: Assigning one list to another (aList = bList) assigns a copy of the list. If bList contains [20, 40, 60], then aList will also contain [20, 40, 60] after the assignment.

content.term: What happens when you access an invalid list index?
content.definition: If a list index is less than 1 or greater than the length of the list, an error message is produced and the program will terminate.

rows: Assigns x to element at index i
Inserts at index i — shifts elements RIGHT
Removes at index i — shifts elements LEFT

content.code:
aList ← [10, 20, 30, 40]

INSERT(aList, 2, 15)
-- Shifts 20,30,40 RIGHT → [10, 15, 20, 30, 40]
-- aList[2] is now 15, aList[3] is now 20

REMOVE(aList, 3)
-- Removes index 3 (value 20), shifts 30,40 LEFT → [10, 15, 30, 40]

APPEND(aList, 99)
-- [10, 15, 30, 40, 99]

DISPLAY LENGTH(aList)  -- 5

content.label: Common Mistakes
content.text: List indices start at 1 in AP CSP — NOT 0. aList[0] causes an error. INSERT shifts elements RIGHT — after inserting at index 2, what was at index 2 is now at index 3. REMOVE shifts elements LEFT — after removing index 3, what was at index 4 is now at index 3. Always retrace the full list after INSERT or REMOVE before reading any element.
Topics 3.3 and 3.4 — Algorithms, Expressions, and Strings

content.definition: A finite set of instructions that accomplishes a specific task. Every algorithm can be constructed using combinations of sequencing, selection, and iteration. Can be expressed in natural language, diagrams, pseudocode, or programming languages.

content.term: Three Building Blocks of Every Algorithm
content.definition:
Sequencing: executing steps in order.
Selection: choosing which steps to execute based on a condition.
Iteration: repeating steps.
The application of each step of an algorithm in the order in which the code statements are given. Sequential statements execute in the order they appear in the code segment.
Addition (+), subtraction (-), multiplication (*), division (/), and MOD. MOD returns the remainder when a is divided by b. Example: 17 MOD 5 = 2. MOD has the same precedence as * and /.
Joins together two or more strings end-to-end to make a new string.
A part of an existing string.

content.code:
-- Order of operations: parentheses, then *, /, MOD left-to-right, then +, -
x ← 2 + 3 * 4       -- x = 14 (not 20)
y ← 10 MOD 3 * 2    -- y = 2  (10 MOD 3 = 1, then 1*2 = 2)
z ← (2 + 3) * 4     -- z = 20 (parentheses first)

-- Division is EXACT:
17 / 5 = 3.4   -- NOT 3

-- MOD:
17 MOD 5 = 2   -- 17 = 3×5 + 2
8 MOD 2 = 0    -- even number check
7 MOD 2 = 1    -- odd number check

-- String concatenation:
concat("Hello", " World")   -- "Hello World"
concat("100", "200")        -- "100200" NOT 300!
-- Concatenation joins text end-to-end, NOT arithmetic

content.label: Exam Tips
content.text: MOD has the SAME precedence as * and / — not lower. Division produces exact decimals: 17/5 = 3.4 not 3. concat("100","200") = "100200" as a string — never 300. Every algorithm can be expressed in natural language, diagrams, pseudocode, or a programming language.
Topic 3.5 — Boolean Expressions

content.definition: A value that is either true or false. Produced by relational operators (=, ≠, >, <, ≥, ≤) and logical operators (NOT, AND, OR).

Used to test the relationship between two variables, expressions, or values. A comparison using a relational operator evaluates to a Boolean value. Operators: = (equal), ≠ (not equal), > (greater than), < (less than), ≥ (greater than or equal), ≤ (less than or equal).

NOT, AND, and OR — each evaluates to a Boolean value.
NOT condition: true if condition is false.
condition1 AND condition2: true only if both are true.
condition1 OR condition2: true if at least one is true.

true AND true = true
true AND false = false
false AND true = false
false AND false = false
AND is only true when BOTH conditions are true.

true OR true = true
true OR false = true
false OR true = true
false OR false = false
OR is only false when BOTH conditions are false.

NOT true = false
NOT false = true
NOT simply flips the Boolean value.

AND: both conditions must be true for the result to be true. If either is false, result is false.
OR: at least one condition must be true for the result to be true. Only false when both conditions are false.

content.code:
x ← 7

-- Evaluating step by step:
(x > 5) AND (x < 10)       -- true AND true = true
(x > 10) OR (x MOD 2 = 1)  -- false OR true = true (7 is odd)
NOT(x = 7)                 -- NOT true = false
(x ≥ 7)                    -- true (7 = 7 satisfies ≥)

-- Common patterns:
x MOD 2 = 0              -- x is even
x MOD 2 = 1              -- x is odd
x MOD n = 0              -- x is divisible by n
(x ≥ a) AND (x ≤ b)      -- x is between a and b inclusive
NOT(x < 15)              -- equivalent to x ≥ 15
(x > 15) OR (x = 15)     -- also equivalent to x ≥ 15

content.label: Exam Tips
content.text: AND: only TRUE when ALL conditions are true. OR: only FALSE when ALL conditions are false. (x ≥ 5) is TRUE when x=5 — the equal part satisfies the condition at the boundary. Always evaluate each relational comparison to true/false first, then apply the logical operators. Equivalent expressions: x ≥ 15 = (x > 15) OR (x = 15) = NOT(x < 15).
Topics 3.6 and 3.7 — Conditionals and Nested Conditionals

content.definition: Determines which parts of an algorithm are executed based on a condition being true or false. Implemented using IF and IF/ELSE statements.

Affects the sequential flow of control by executing different statements based on the value of a Boolean expression. IF(condition): executes the block only if condition is true. IF/ELSE: executes the first block if true, the second block if false.
Conditional statements within conditional statements. Allow programs to check multiple conditions in sequence, where inner conditions are only evaluated if outer conditions are met.

content.label: Common Mistake
content.text: Multiple separate IFs are ALL evaluated — a value satisfying 3 conditions produces 3 outputs. An IF/ELSE produces exactly ONE output. In nested conditionals: the inner IF is NEVER evaluated if the outer condition sends execution to the ELSE branch. Always trace OUTSIDE-IN.
Topic 3.8 — Iteration

content.definition: A repeating portion of an algorithm. REPEAT n TIMES executes a block n times. REPEAT UNTIL(condition) repeats until the condition is true — if already true, the block never executes. An infinite loop occurs if the condition never becomes true.
An iteration statement that executes the block of statements exactly n times.

An iteration statement that repeats the block of statements until the Boolean condition evaluates to true. If the condition is true initially, the loop body is not executed at all. If the condition never becomes true, an infinite loop occurs.
Occurs in REPEAT UNTIL iteration when the ending condition will never evaluate to true, causing the loop to repeat forever.

content.term: Compare: REPEAT n TIMES vs REPEAT UNTIL
content.definition:
REPEAT n TIMES: repeats a fixed number of times, always executes the block at least once if n > 0.
REPEAT UNTIL: repeats until a condition becomes true, may not execute at all if the condition is already true.

content.term: What happens when REPEAT UNTIL condition is already true?
content.definition: The loop body is not executed at all, because the condition is checked before the loop begins.

content.code:
-- REPEAT n TIMES: always exactly n iterations
REPEAT 5 TIMES { DISPLAY "hello" }   -- displays hello 5 times

-- REPEAT UNTIL: condition checked BEFORE each iteration
i ← 1
REPEAT UNTIL(i > 5)
{
   DISPLAY i    -- displays 1 2 3 4 5
   i ← i + 1
}

-- Condition already true → ZERO iterations:
x ← 10
REPEAT UNTIL(x = 10) { x ← x + 1 }   -- body never runs, x stays 10
DISPLAY x   -- displays 10

-- Infinite loop — condition never becomes true:
x ← 0
REPEAT UNTIL(x = 5)
{
   x ← x + 2   -- x goes 0,2,4,6... NEVER equals exactly 5
}

rows: Until condition true — could be 0 or many
YES — if condition already true at start
YES — if condition never becomes true

content.label: Exam Tips
content.text: REPEAT UNTIL checks BEFORE executing — if condition is already true, the body executes ZERO times. Always check that the loop variable is updated inside the body to eventually make the condition true — forgetting this causes infinite loops. x starts at 0, adds 2 each time, condition x=5 → INFINITE LOOP (skips from 4 to 6).
Topic 3.9 — Developing Algorithms

content.term: Can different algorithms solve the same problem?
content.definition: Yes. Algorithms can be written in different ways and still accomplish the same task. However, algorithms that appear similar can yield different side effects or results. Different algorithms can also have different efficiencies.

content.term: How can new algorithms be created?
content.definition: Algorithms can be created from an idea, by combining existing algorithms, or by modifying existing algorithms. Using existing correct algorithms as building blocks reduces development time, reduces testing, and simplifies error identification.

Determining the maximum or minimum value of two or more numbers, computing the sum or average of numbers, identifying if an integer is evenly divisible by another integer, determining a robot's path through a maze.

content.term: Can algorithms that look similar produce different results?
content.definition: Yes. Algorithms that appear similar can yield different side effects or results. The order and structure of statements matters — even small differences can change the outcome.

content.term: Can conditional statements and Boolean expressions be equivalent?
content.definition: Yes. Some conditional statements can be written as equivalent Boolean expressions, and some Boolean expressions can be written as equivalent conditional statements.

content.code:
-- CRITICAL: algorithms that look similar can produce DIFFERENT results

-- Algorithm A (WRONG for all-negative lists):
max ← 0
FOR EACH item IN aList { IF(item > max) { max ← item } }
-- For [-5, -3, -8]: returns 0 ← WRONG (0 is not in the list)

-- Algorithm B (ALWAYS CORRECT):
max ← aList[1]    -- initialize to FIRST ELEMENT, not 0
FOR EACH item IN aList { IF(item > max) { max ← item } }
-- For [-5, -3, -8]: returns -3 ← correct
-- For [5, 3, 8]: returns 8 ← also correct

-- Using existing algorithms as building blocks:
-- Average algorithm = sum algorithm + division step
-- Benefits: reduces development time, reduces testing,
--           simplifies identification of errors

content.text: Topic 3.10 — Lists

content.definition:
ACCESS: aList[i] — gets element at index i.
ASSIGN: aList[i] = x — sets element at index i to x.
INSERT(aList, i, value) — inserts value at index i, shifting elements right.
APPEND(aList, value) — adds value to end of list.
REMOVE(aList, i) — removes element at index i, shifting elements left.
LENGTH(aList) — returns number of elements.

Accessing elements of a list one by one. Can be complete (all elements accessed) or partial (only some elements accessed). FOR EACH item IN aList assigns each element to item sequentially from first to last and executes the block once per element.

Traverses a list by assigning each element to a variable sequentially from first to last. The block of statements executes once for each element. Note: parallel traversals (using the same index for two lists simultaneously) are outside the scope of AP CSP.
Finding the minimum or maximum value in a list, computing the sum or average of a list of numbers. These existing algorithms can be used as building blocks when constructing new algorithms.
An algorithm that checks each element of a list in order until the desired value is found or all elements have been checked.

content.label: Common Mistake
content.text: ALWAYS initialize max/min to aList[1] — the first element — NOT to 0. Initializing to 0 fails for any list containing only negative numbers (returns 0, which is not in the list). Initialize sum to 0. In FOR EACH linear search, the loop continues through ALL elements even after finding the target — found stays true once set.
Topic 3.11 — Binary Search

content.definition: An algorithm that starts at the middle of a sorted data set and eliminates half of the remaining data with each step. Repeats until the desired value is found or all elements have been eliminated. Data must be in sorted order to use binary search.

content.term: Compare: Linear Search vs Binary Search
content.definition:
Linear search: checks each element one by one, works on unsorted data, less efficient for large data sets.
Binary search: eliminates half the data each step, requires sorted data, often more efficient than linear search on sorted data.

content.term: What makes binary search more efficient than linear search?
content.definition: Binary search eliminates half the remaining data with each step, while linear search checks one element at a time. Binary search is often more efficient on sorted data, but requires the data to be sorted first.

rows: Checks one element at a time from the start
Starts at middle, eliminates half each step

content.label: Exam Tip
content.text: Binary search REQUIRES sorted data — cannot be used on an unsorted list without sorting first. If asked 'which search works on unsorted data?' the answer is ONLY linear search. Specific implementations of binary search are outside the scope of the exam — understand the concept, not the code.
Topics 3.12 and 3.13 — Calling and Developing Procedures

content.definition: A named group of programming instructions that may have parameters and return values. Also called a method or function. A procedure call interrupts sequential execution — flow returns to the calling point after the procedure finishes.

Parameters: input variables defined in the procedure declaration.
Arguments: actual values passed when the procedure is called. Each argument is assigned to its corresponding parameter.

content.term: What happens when a procedure is called?
content.definition: A procedure call interrupts sequential execution and causes the program to execute the statements within the procedure. Once the last statement or a RETURN statement executes, flow of control returns to the point immediately following where the procedure was called.
Returns the flow of control to the point where the procedure was called and returns the value of an expression. May appear at any point inside a procedure and causes an immediate return.

DISPLAY(expression): displays the value of expression followed by a space.
INPUT(): accepts a value from the user and returns the input value.

Provides a name for a process and allows a procedure to be used knowing only what it does, not how it does it. Enables code reuse, improves readability, and allows internals to be changed without affecting users as long as behavior is preserved.
The subdivision of a computer program into separate subprograms. Using parameters allows procedures to be generalized and reused with different inputs.

Allows code reuse by extracting shared features instead of duplicating code. Improves readability. Using parameters allows procedures to be generalized and reused with different inputs. Allows programmers to change internals of a procedure without notifying users as long as the behavior is preserved.

content.term: Why can procedural abstraction be changed without affecting users?
content.definition: Programmers can change the internals of a procedure (make it faster, more efficient, use less storage) without notifying users of the change, as long as what the procedure does is preserved.

content.label: Exam Tips
content.text: Arguments assigned to parameters IN ORDER — first to first, second to second. RETURN causes IMMEDIATE exit — code after a RETURN in the same branch never executes. For nested calls, evaluate the innermost call first. Procedural abstraction benefits: (1) code reuse, (2) improved readability, (3) generalization through parameters, (4) internals can change without affecting users.
Topic 3.14 — Libraries

content.definition: A collection of procedures that may be used in creating new programs. Simplifies creating complex programs. An API specifies how the procedures in a library behave and can be used.

Application Program Interface — a specification for how the procedures in a library behave and can be used. Documentation for an API is necessary to understand the behaviors provided and how to use them.

content.text: Existing code segments can come from internal sources (your own previous code) or external sources (libraries, other developers). API documentation is necessary to understand what procedures are available, what parameters they take, what they return, and how to use them correctly. Using a library is procedural abstraction in practice — you use its procedures knowing WHAT they do, not HOW.
Topic 3.15 — Random Values

content.definition: Generates and returns a random integer from a to b, inclusive. Each result is equally likely to occur. Example: RANDOM(1, 3) could return 1, 2, or 3. Using random number generation means each execution may produce a different result.

content.code:
RANDOM(1, 6)   -- returns 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6 (each with prob 1/6)
RANDOM(1, 2)   -- returns 1 or 2 (50% each) — coin flip
RANDOM(1, 4)   -- P(any specific value) = 1/4 = 25%

-- Number of possible values = b - a + 1
-- P(any specific value) = 1 / (b - a + 1)
-- RANDOM(3, 7): 5 values → P(any one) = 1/5 = 20%

-- Random list element (valid index 1 to length):
index ← RANDOM(1, LENGTH(aList))
DISPLAY aList[index]

-- Each run may produce DIFFERENT results — programs with RANDOM are non-deterministic

content.label: Exam Tips
content.text: RANDOM generates INTEGERS only — never decimals. Both endpoints (a and b) are possible results. Each result is equally likely. Use RANDOM(1, LENGTH(aList)) for a valid random index — NEVER RANDOM(0,...) because index 0 is invalid in AP CSP.
Topic 3.16 — Simulations

content.definition: An abstraction of a more complex object or phenomenon for a specific purpose. Most useful when real-world events are impractical (too big, small, fast, slow, expensive, or dangerous). Can contain bias from elements included or excluded. Random number generators simulate real-world variability.
When real-world events are impractical for experiments — too big, too small, too fast, too slow, too expensive, or too dangerous. Simulations facilitate the formulation and refinement of hypotheses.
Developing a simulation involves removing specific details or simplifying functionality. Simulations can contain bias derived from the choices of real-world elements that were included or excluded.

content.term: How do simulations use random values?
content.definition: Random number generators can be used in simulations to simulate the variability that exists in the real world, making the simulation more realistic.

rows: Mountain formation over millions of years

content.label: Key Ideas
content.text: Simulations are ABSTRACTIONS — they simplify reality by removing details. They can contain BIAS from what was included or excluded. A simulation being imperfect does NOT make it useless — all simulations simplify reality and still provide valuable insights. Simulations facilitate formulation and refinement of hypotheses. Random number generators add the variability that exists in the real world.
Topic 3.17 — Algorithmic Efficiency

content.definition: An estimation of computational resources used by an algorithm, typically expressed as a function of input size. Reasonable: polynomial efficiency or slower (constant, linear, square, cube). Unreasonable: exponential or factorial efficiency.

content.term: How is algorithmic efficiency informally measured?
content.definition: By determining the number of times a statement or group of statements executes. Different correct algorithms for the same problem can have different efficiencies.

Reasonable: polynomial efficiency or slower — constant, linear, square, cube, etc.
Unreasonable: exponential or factorial efficiency — these algorithms take too long to be practical for large inputs.

An approach to a problem that produces a solution that is not guaranteed to be optimal but may be used when techniques guaranteed to find an optimal solution are impractical. Used when a problem cannot be solved in reasonable time.

content.term: Compare: Decision Problem vs Optimization Problem
content.definition:
Decision problem: has a yes/no answer (e.g. Is there a path from A to B?).
Optimization problem: goal is to find the best solution among many (e.g. What is the shortest path from A to B?).

content.term: Problem vs Instance of a Problem
content.definition: A problem is a general description of a task (e.g. sorting). An instance of a problem includes specific input (e.g. sorting the list [2, 3, 1, 7]). Some problems cannot be solved in a reasonable amount of time — in these cases approximate solutions are sought.

rows: Always the same regardless of n

content.label: Exam Tips
content.text: Reasonable = POLYNOMIAL (constant, linear, n², n³). Unreasonable = EXPONENTIAL or FACTORIAL. A heuristic produces a GOOD but NOT GUARANTEED optimal solution — used when exact algorithms are impractical. Decision problem → yes/no answer. Optimization problem → find the best solution. Formal Big-O notation and specific heuristic algorithms are outside the scope of the exam.
Topic 3.18 — Undecidable Problems

content.definition: A decision problem for which an algorithm can be written to produce a correct output for all inputs. Example: Is the number even?

A problem for which no algorithm can be constructed that is always capable of providing a correct yes-or-no answer. An undecidable problem may have some instances with an algorithmic solution, but no single algorithm can solve all instances.

Decidable: an algorithm exists that always produces a correct yes/no answer for all inputs.
Undecidable: no algorithm can always produce a correct yes/no answer for all inputs. Some instances may be solvable but not all.

content.text: The Halting Problem asks: will a given program halt for a given input? Alan Turing proved no algorithm can correctly answer this for ALL possible programs and inputs. This is not a limitation of computing power — it is a mathematical proof that no such algorithm can ever exist. An undecidable problem may have some specific instances with algorithmic solutions — but no SINGLE algorithm works for all instances.

rows: NO — mathematical proof, not hardware limit

content.label: Common Mistake
content.text: Undecidable ≠ unreasonable running time. Unreasonable = algorithm EXISTS but too slow. Undecidable = NO algorithm can EVER exist for all inputs. Quantum computers, future technology, more processing power — NONE of these can solve an undecidable problem for all inputs. It is a mathematical impossibility, not a hardware limitation. Determining whether a given problem is undecidable is outside the scope of the exam.
How Unit 3 Fits Together

rows: How do programs store single values and collections? Variables, lists, and data abstraction.
How do programs compute results and work with text? Arithmetic, MOD, and string operations.
How do programs test conditions? Relational and logical operators producing true/false values.
How do programs make decisions and repeat? IF/ELSE, nested conditionals, REPEAT loops.
How do programs process data collections? Building list algorithms and searching efficiently.
How do programs manage complexity? Named procedures, parameters, libraries, and APIs.
How do programs model the real world? RANDOM values and simulations as abstractions.
What can and cannot algorithms do? Efficiency categories, heuristics, and undecidability.

String: ordered sequence of characters; concat joins strings end-to-end; substring is a consecutive part
concat("100","200") = "100200" as a string — NOT arithmetic addition

Sequencing: statements execute in the order they appear

x ≥ 5 is TRUE when x=5 — boundary satisfies ≥. x > 5 is FALSE when x=5.
Selection: IF executes when true, skips when false; IF/ELSE executes exactly one block
Multiple separate IFs all evaluated; IF/ELSE stops at first true; nested conditionals: inner evaluated only when outer allows
Iteration: REPEAT n TIMES = exactly n; REPEAT UNTIL checks condition BEFORE each iteration

Algorithms can be created from ideas, by combining, or by modifying existing algorithms

Algorithms that look similar can produce DIFFERENT results — initialization matters enormously
ALWAYS initialize max/min to aList[1] — NEVER to 0 (fails for all-negative lists)
FOR EACH traverses all elements first to last — complete or partial
Linear search: one by one, works on any list. Binary search: halves each step, MUST be sorted.
Binary search for n elements: at most log₂(n) steps vs up to n for linear
Procedure: named group of instructions with parameters and return values
Parameters in declaration; arguments in call — assigned in ORDER (first to first)
Procedure call interrupts sequential execution — flow returns to calling point after procedure finishes
RETURN exits immediately and returns value — can appear ANYWHERE in the procedure
Procedural abstraction: use a procedure knowing WHAT it does, not HOW
Benefits: code reuse, improved readability, generalization through parameters, internals can change without affecting users
Modularity: subdivide programs into subprograms — parameters allow generalization for different inputs
Software library: collection of procedures for creating programs; API specifies how to use them
API documentation is NECESSARY to understand what procedures do and how to use them correctly
RANDOM(a, b): random INTEGER from a to b inclusive — integers only, each equally likely
P(specific value from RANDOM(a,b)) = 1/(b-a+1); each run may produce DIFFERENT results
Use RANDOM(1, LENGTH(aList)) for valid random index — NEVER RANDOM(0,...)
Simulation: abstraction of a complex phenomenon — uses varying values to reflect changing state
Most useful when real experiments impractical: too big, small, fast, slow, expensive, dangerous
Simulations can contain BIAS from choices about what was included or excluded
Simulations being imperfect does NOT make them useless — they still provide valuable insights
Random number generators simulate variability that exists in the real world
Algorithmic efficiency: estimation of computational resources as function of input size
Reasonable: polynomial (constant, linear, n², n³); Unreasonable: exponential or factorial
Efficiency measured informally by counting how many times a statement executes
Some problems have no efficient algorithm — heuristics find good but not guaranteed optimal solutions
Decision problem: yes/no answer. Optimization problem: find the best solution.
Decidable: algorithm always gives correct yes/no for ALL inputs
Undecidable: NO algorithm can always give correct yes/no for ALL inputs — some instances may be solvable
